summary: Describes a method for random selection whose unbiased nature is publicly verifiable, using selection of NomCom voting members from volunteers as the example. It obsoletes RFC 2777. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Picking names from a hat is fair only if everyone can check it. This describes a way to pick at random that anyone can check afterward.

questions: how are nomcom members chosen randomly
what is publicly verifiable random selection
how does the nomcom selection algorithm work
subtitle: How to pick people at random so that anyone can check afterwards that nobody cheated.

tldr.problem: Each year ten people are randomly chosen from eligible volunteers to be voting members of the IETF Nominations Committee, and the draw must be beyond reproach.
tldr.mechanism: Publish the volunteer list and the exact algorithm first, base the choice on public future random sources such as lotteries, and mix them with an MD5 hash to pick people in order.
tldr.outcome: Anyone can rerun the calculation from public data and confirm the result. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2777 and is Informational.

today: RFC 3797 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 2777. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Selection Must Be Verifiable
sections.content:
Under the IETF rules, each year ten people are randomly selected from eligible volunteers to be the voting members of the IETF Nominations Committee (NomCom), which nominates members of the IESG and the IAB. The RFC says the pool has been around 100 volunteers in recent years.

The draw should be unimpeachable, so that no reasonable charge of bias or favoritism can be made. That protects the selection administrator as much as the IETF. A method where public information lets any person verify the randomness meets this goal. The method was also used by IANA in February 2003 to pick the ACE prefix for Internationalized Domain Names.
sections.plainLanguage: If a teacher picks helpers, kids may wonder if it was fair. If the way of picking is written down first and anyone can redo it, nobody has to wonder.

sections.title: The Three Steps and the Source of Randomness
sections.content:
A publicly verifiable process has three steps. First, determine and publish the pool of eligible volunteers early enough to settle any disputes. Second, publish the exact algorithm, including the future sources of randomness. Third, when those sources produce their output, announce the values and a summary of the run so that anyone can check it. The algorithm can select more people than needed, in order, to provide alternates, and a cut-off time for complaints must be set.

The key idea is that the choice depends in a fixed way on random data that will be revealed in the future, so the person writing the algorithm cannot know it. The sources must not be anything a reasonable person would think the IETF could influence, such as meeting attendance statistics.

Good sources are winning numbers of specified public lotteries. Stock prices and volumes proved a poor source because of suspensions, splits and similar events. The last source in time should supply much of the entropy, so nobody with limited influence over it can bias the result. Three or four sources is a good number, and ten is too many.
sections.plainLanguage: Write the rules down and choose something nobody can know yet, like tomorrow's lottery numbers. Then nobody can rig the draw, because nobody knows the answer ahead of time.

sections.title: The Suggested Algorithm
sections.content:
Each source's numbers are written as decimals ending in a period, sorted from smallest to largest, concatenated, and suffixed with /. The strings for all sources are joined in a fixed order to form one key string. Sorting matters because the same lottery results may be reported in drawing order or numeric order.

The key string is then hashed with MD5, prefixed and suffixed by a two-byte big-endian counter (0x0000 for the first value, 0x0001 for the second, and so on). Each 128-bit result is read as a big-endian integer. With P volunteers, the first pick is the remainder of the first value divided by P, plus one, as a position in the published list. The second divides by P-1 over the list with the first person removed, and so on.

The RFC strongly recommends avoiding alphanumeric sources because they are hard to canonicalize identically. It computes that 40 bits of entropy is adequate for the pool sizes likely to occur, and it says a stronger hash such as SHA-1 can be used if desired.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone's numbers get mixed together in a blender that always gives the same smoothie from the same ingredients. The smoothie tells you which names to pick, and anyone can run the same blender.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC works through a fake example with 25 volunteers and three invented sources: a four-digit lottery number, horse-race results, and six lottery numbers. The key string is 9319./2.5.8.10.12./9.18.26.34.41.45./. The first ten selected, in order, are Lee (17), Doc (7), Mary (2), Charity (16), Kasczynski (25), Envy (23), Sneazy (8), Anger (24), Chastity (19) and Pandora (13). If one declined or was ineligible, the next would be Sloth, number 22.

Section 8 of the RFC also includes C reference code that implements the method. It supports pools up to 2**16-1 members.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is like a pretend raffle with made-up numbers. It shows step by step how the same numbers always lead to the same winners.

sections.title: Real-World Problems
sections.content:
Section 5 covers problems that actually arose. If it is uncertain whether someone is eligible, keep the schedule, include them in the published pool, and keep the numbering immutable. If such a person is selected and turns out to be ineligible, skip them and run the algorithm further. Inserting or deleting entries after publication changes the list length and can scramble every selection.

If a random source is ambiguous when the time comes, for example a volume published in hundreds instead of thousands, announcing new sources would raise suspicion. The only option is to make a reasonable choice and rely on the administrator's good faith. This is why the RFC again recommends public lottery numbers and avoiding stock prices and volumes.
sections.plainLanguage: If the list of kids changes after the draw starts, everything gets scrambled. So the list is locked first, and anyone doubtful stays on it and is just skipped if picked.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The inputs must be chosen so that no reasonable person suspects the administrator controls them. The advice is to use a small number of inputs, with a substantial amount of entropy from the last. The algorithm must also be executed faithfully with the designated values. Publishing the results and allowing a week or so for the community to repeat the calculations gives reasonable assurance against tampering.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick things nobody in charge can touch, then give everyone a week to check the math.
